When you are more concerned with other people's gameplay rather than your own, you aren't exactly looking to improve.

I wouldn't necessarily agree, sometimes when you're really skilled you can have a larger awareness as to how things are going and you can tell when someone isn't pulling their weight, while this will be difficult in online games with a bunch of randos, but if you're playing in a area that you can see just about everything with a small enough number of people you can pay attention to how everything is playing out, and as a result you can determine when others aren't pulling their own weight. For example, when I play a Tales of game I have to stay on top of everything that's going on because the AI on my team is sometimes abysmal, and since I play on the hardest difficulty we have to manage the battle field precisely or else any boss will just tear through us, while I'm certainly not perfect the idiot AI that does't understand how to run away or constantly attack is a major drain on the TP, items, and what have you so I tend to have to be extra critical of their faults in order to best figure out how to tweak their AI or my strategy to better suit what they can do and the challenge we're up against, similarly I've seen several of my friends who are experienced with monster hunter holding a somewhat similar awareness as to how even I play when we group together for the same sorta reasons. When you're good you're able to notice how others can improve, so being more concerned with how the weakest link on your team is functioning is simply the best way to update strategies or find a way to make sure that you don't all get wiped out.

However, even with this, I usually don't see people getting hugely angry about things, perhaps frustrated that the enemy keeps managing to take advantage of the weakness, but usually never yelling (well I might, but that's to computers because there is literally no way to manipulate the AI to have them use free-run to avoid attacks, constantly attack, or keep switching between enemies to help keep the mages protected), the biggest thing that usually fuels yelling is getting massively frustrated with losing either in short term (deaths in a match) or long term (match results), so the people who will be the most frustrated and thus willing to yell will probably be the ones who just aren't good since they'll be dieing more and losing more then a skilled player whom has team awareness.
What Tales of game? Talesofgame.com or something? This is bothering me : D

'Tales of' is a series of games, some of the more popular titles include 'Tales of Symphonia' (I really love the title system in that one), 'Tales of Vesperia', and recently 'Tales of Xillia'. They're all action RPG games, in them you have up to 4 characters fighting at a time but you as a player only control the actions of one of them at a time (if you choose to), most of the games allow other players to control other characters as well but if you're like me and have to play alone you'll have to rely on a customizable AI to control whatever characters you don't. You'll be able to switch between them (though in some of the games you have to get the 'Moon selector' key item first) and most of them you have a level of customization over your party in terms of artes (attack skills/spells), skills (passives), and titles (affects vary between games) which adds an element of puzzle solving to my team setup for the bosses that I absolutely love, but on the challenging fights you're going to have to be able to read the enemies and respond appropriately, so there is fair amount of skill that comes into play too.

If you're interested in trying one out I'd advise trying out either Vesperia or Xillia since they're some of the best (I'd advise against anything before Abyss to start with, aside from Symphonia they all have 2D battle areas, and Symphonia doesn't have free-run), and maybe try to avoid playing on the easiest setting (at least once you've got a team you're happy with, try experimenting with the team members some though, I've found that some characters have smarter AI than others), in my experience the easiest setting it's pretty easy to just go straight through the game relying on having your numbers being better then the enemy numbers, as you up the difficulties that becomes less viable so you instead have to rely on good skill, strategy, and being able to use your team properly. Most of my playthroughs I usually end up making a ton of save files so that I have files before almost every boss so that I can go back and fight the REALLY fun ones again.

Introducing our (formerly) terrified rescue boys, Jacques and Basil.

Jacques and Basil came to us as young rats (maybe around 3-4 months old) from our local rescue centre at the end of April. These poor wee guys had been abandoned in a layby over Easter weekend; they were terrified and completely unhandleable, drawing a fair amount of blood any time we tried to feed them or give them treats. It's taken a lot of TLC, patience (and plasters/band aids) to bring them round and help them realise they're now in their "forever home".

Jacques is still ill (3 weeks and 3 separate medications haven't shifted the myco), but they're no longer drawing blood from us when we try to fuzzle them. They now come to us for hugs when we open their cage, so they've come on leaps and bounds...literally, as it happens!
